messages.content: What is the central innovation introduced in the Attention Is All You Need paper?

The central innovation is the Transformer, a sequence transduction model that relies entirely on attention mechanisms and completely dispenses with recurrence and convolutions. Before the Transformer, the dominant approaches used recurrent neural networks (LSTMs, GRUs) as their backbone, which process sequences step-by-step and cannot be parallelised within a training example. The Transformer replaces that sequential computation with multi-head self-attention, allowing every position in a sequence to attend to every other position in a constant number of operations. The result is a model that is significantly more parallelisable, trains faster, and achieves higher translation quality than prior architectures.
What fundamental limitation of recurrent neural networks does the Transformer address?

Recurrent neural networks compute hidden states sequentially: h_t depends on h_{t-1} and the input at position t. This inherently sequential nature prevents parallelisation within a single training example. At longer sequence lengths, memory constraints also limit how many examples can be batched together. Attention mechanisms had already been used with RNNs to model long-range dependencies, but they were always paired with a recurrent backbone. The Transformer removes the recurrent backbone entirely, replacing it with self-attention so that all positions can be processed in parallel, reducing training time from days to hours for large translation models while improving quality.
Describe the encoder architecture of the Transformer.

The Transformer encoder is a stack of N=6 identical layers. Each layer contains exactly two sub-layers: (1) a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and (2) a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. A residual connection is applied around each sub-layer, followed by layer normalisation. Concretely, each sub-layer computes LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). To make the residual connections work cleanly, every sub-layer and the embedding layers all produce outputs of the same dimension d_model=512. The encoder processes the entire input sequence in parallel, and every position attends to every other position in the previous layer.
How does the Transformer decoder differ from the encoder?

The decoder is also a stack of N=6 identical layers, but each layer has three sub-layers instead of two. The extra sub-layer is an encoder-decoder attention layer that performs multi-head attention over the encoder output, allowing each decoder position to attend to all input sequence positions. The self-attention sub-layer in the decoder is also modified: it uses masking to prevent any position from attending to subsequent (future) positions. This masking, combined with the fact that output embeddings are shifted by one position, ensures the auto-regressive property: predictions at position i can only depend on outputs at positions less than i. Both sub-layers are wrapped with the same residual connections and layer normalisation as in the encoder.
Explain Scaled Dot-Product Attention and its formula.

Scaled Dot-Product Attention takes three inputs: queries Q, keys K, and values V. The output is computed as: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V. The steps are: (1) compute the dot products of each query with all keys to get compatibility scores, (2) divide each score by sqrt(d_k) to prevent the softmax from entering a region of extremely small gradients when d_k is large, (3) apply softmax to convert scores to weights, and (4) take a weighted sum of the values. The scaling by 1/sqrt(d_k) is critical because for large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude - if the components of q and k have mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance d_k, pushing softmax into near-zero gradient regions.
Why does the paper scale dot products by 1/sqrt(dk) in the attention formula?

For large values of d_k, the dot products between queries and keys grow large in magnitude. If the components of a query vector q and key vector k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, then their dot product q·k = sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i has mean 0 and variance d_k. When d_k is large these large dot products push the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients, making learning very slow or stalling it entirely. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) brings the variance back to 1, keeping softmax in a numerically stable, high-gradient region throughout training. The authors note that additive attention does not suffer this problem and actually outperforms dot-product attention without scaling for large d_k.
What is Multi-Head Attention and why is it used instead of single-head attention?

Multi-Head Attention projects queries, keys and values h times with different learned linear projections, runs attention on each projected version in parallel, then concatenates the results and projects once more. Formally: MultiHead(Q,K,V) = Concat(head_1,...,head_h) W^O, where head_i = Attention(Q W^Q_i, K W^K_i, V W^V_i). In the base model h=8 heads, and d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 64. With a single attention head, averaging over all positions inhibits the model from jointly attending to information from different representation subspaces. With 8 independent heads, each can specialise - some learn syntactic relationships, others semantic ones. Since each head works in a reduced 64-dimensional space, the total computation is similar to a single full-dimensional attention operation.
In what three distinct ways is multi-head attention used within the Transformer?

The Transformer uses multi-head attention in three ways. First, encoder self-attention: all queries, keys and values come from the output of the previous encoder layer, so every position can attend to every other position in the previous encoder layer. Second, decoder self-attention (masked): same structure as encoder self-attention but future positions are masked out (set to -infinity before softmax) to preserve the auto-regressive property. Third, encoder-decoder attention: queries come from the previous decoder layer while keys and values come from the encoder output, allowing every decoder position to attend over all positions in the input sequence - the classic cross-attention pattern from sequence-to-sequence models.
Why does the Transformer need positional encodings, and what formula is used?

Because the Transformer contains no recurrence and no convolution, it has no inherent sense of token order. A sequence scrambled in any order would produce the same attention weights without position information. Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings at the bottom of both encoder and decoder stacks. The paper uses sinusoidal encodings: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model)) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model)). Wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2*pi to 10000*2*pi. The key advantage over learned positional embeddings is that sinusoidal encodings can extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training, since PE_{pos+k} can be represented as a linear function of PE_{pos} for any fixed offset k.
What is the Position-wise Feed-Forward Network in the Transformer?

Each layer in both encoder and decoder contains a position-wise feed-forward network (FFN) applied identically and independently at each position. It consists of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between: FFN(x) = max(0, x W_1 + b_1) W_2 + b_2. The input and output dimension is d_model=512, while the inner hidden layer dimension is d_ff=2048. The same linear transformation is used across positions within a layer, but different parameters are used across layers. This FFN provides the bulk of the model capacity for mixing information at each position after the attention sub-layer has aggregated context from across the sequence. It is equivalent to two convolutions with kernel size 1.
How does self-attention compare to recurrent layers in computational complexity and path length?

The paper compares three layer types on three criteria. (1) Complexity per layer: Self-attention is O(n^2 * d) vs Recurrent O(n * d^2). Self-attention is faster when n < d, which holds for sentence-length sequences with d=512. (2) Sequential operations: Self-attention requires O(1) sequential operations (all positions computed in parallel); recurrent layers require O(n). (3) Maximum path length: Self-attention connects any two positions in O(1) steps, making long-range dependency learning much easier. Recurrent layers require O(n) steps. Convolutional layers need O(log_k(n)) (dilated) or O(n/k) (contiguous) stacked layers. O(1) path length is why the Transformer is particularly effective at capturing long-range dependencies compared to LSTM-based models.
What training data and batching strategy did the Transformer use?

For English-to-German translation the Transformer was trained on the WMT 2014 English-German dataset of approximately 4.5 million sentence pairs, encoded using byte-pair encoding (BPE) with a shared vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens. For English-to-French, the larger WMT 2014 dataset of 36 million sentence pairs was used with a 32,000 word-piece vocabulary. Sentence pairs were batched by approximate sequence length. Each training batch contained approximately 25,000 source tokens and 25,000 target tokens. Training used 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model was trained for 100,000 steps (~12 hours); the big model for 300,000 steps (~3.5 days).
What optimizer and learning rate schedule were used to train the Transformer?

The Transformer used the Adam optimizer with beta_1=0.9, beta_2=0.98, and epsilon=1e-9. The learning rate varied according to: lrate = d_model^{-0.5} * min(step_num^{-0.5}, step_num * warmup_steps^{-1.5}). This increases the learning rate linearly for the first warmup_steps=4000 training steps, then decreases it proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number. The warmup phase is critical: at the start of training, gradients are noisy and jumping to a high learning rate can push parameters into poor regions. The warmup allows the model to reach a reasonable parameter region before the rate decays. The peak learning rate is proportional to d_model^{-0.5}, so smaller models use a higher peak rate.
What regularization techniques were applied during Transformer training?

Three types of regularization were used. (1) Residual Dropout: applied to the output of each sub-layer before it is added to the sub-layer input and normalised, and to the sums of embeddings and positional encodings in both encoder and decoder. The base model used P_drop=0.1; the big EN-FR model used P_drop=0.3. (2) Label Smoothing: during training, label smoothing of epsilon_ls=0.1 was applied. Rather than training to output probability 1.0 for the correct token, the target is smoothed - 0.9 for the correct token and 0.1 spread uniformly across other tokens. This hurts perplexity (the model is more uncertain) but improves accuracy and BLEU score by reducing overconfidence and overfitting.
What were the key benchmark results achieved by the Transformer on machine translation?

On the WMT 2014 English-to-German task, the big Transformer achieved 28.4 BLEU, surpassing all prior models including ensembles by more than 2 BLEU points. The base model also outperformed all previous single models and ensembles. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French task, the big model achieved 41.8 BLEU - a new single-model state-of-the-art at less than 1/4 the training cost of the previous best model. The big model was trained for 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs. For inference, beam search with beam size 4 and length penalty alpha=0.6 was used. Base model checkpoints were averaged (last 5); big model checkpoints averaged (last 20).
What are the key hyperparameters of the base Transformer model?

The base Transformer has: N=6 encoder and decoder layers; d_model=512 (model dimension); d_ff=2048 (FFN inner dimension); h=8 attention heads; d_k=d_v=64 (attention key/value dimension per head); P_drop=0.1 (dropout rate); epsilon_ls=0.1 (label smoothing); warmup_steps=4000; training for 100,000 steps on 8 P100 GPUs. Total parameters: approximately 65 million. The big model uses d_model=1024, d_ff=4096, h=16, P_drop=0.3, 300,000 steps, approximately 213 million parameters.
How did the Transformer perform on English constituency parsing?

To test generalisation beyond translation, the authors applied a 4-layer Transformer with d_model=1024 to English constituency parsing on the Penn Treebank WSJ dataset (~40K training sentences). In the WSJ-only discriminative setting, the Transformer achieved 91.3 F1 on Section 23, competitive with prior state of the art. In the semi-supervised setting using ~17M additional sentences, it achieved 92.7 F1, outperforming all prior models except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar (93.3 F1). This was achieved with minimal task-specific tuning - the model used nearly the same hyperparameters as the translation model, demonstrating that the Transformer's learned representations generalise across different NLP tasks.
How does the Transformer enforce the auto-regressive property during training?

The auto-regressive property requires that the prediction at position i depends only on outputs at positions less than i. The Transformer enforces this through two mechanisms. First, the decoder input (teacher-forced targets) is shifted right by one position, so position i receives the ground-truth token at position i-1. Second, decoder self-attention masks out all future positions: values in the attention logit matrix corresponding to positions j >= i are set to -infinity before the softmax, so they receive zero weight after softmax. These two mechanisms together ensure no information from future positions is available when computing the output at position i, even though the entire sequence is processed in parallel during training.
How are embeddings handled in the Transformer and what weight sharing is used?

Learned embeddings convert input tokens and output tokens to vectors of dimension d_model=512. A learned linear transformation followed by softmax converts decoder outputs to predicted next-token probabilities. The same weight matrix is shared between the two embedding layers (encoder input and decoder input) and the pre-softmax linear transformation - a three-way weight tying that reduces total parameters and has been shown to improve language model quality. In the embedding layers, the shared weights are multiplied by sqrt(d_model) before being summed with positional encodings. This scaling ensures embeddings are not dominated by the positional encoding signal when d_model is large.
What evidence does the paper give that attention heads learn interpretable patterns?

The paper presents attention visualisations from encoder self-attention at layer 5 of 6. Figure 3 shows many attention heads attending to the distant dependency of the verb 'making' in the phrase 'making...more difficult', demonstrating that individual heads track long-range syntactic structure. Figure 4 shows two heads apparently involved in anaphora resolution: for the word 'its', attention is very sharp and focused on the antecedent noun 'Law'. Figure 5 shows additional examples. The conclusion is that individual attention heads clearly learn to perform different tasks, many exhibiting behaviour related to the syntactic and semantic structure of sentences. This interpretability is listed as a beneficial side effect of self-attention.
How do convolutional sequence models like ConvS2S compare to the Transformer?

Convolutional models like ByteNet, ConvS2S, and Extended Neural GPU compute hidden representations in parallel for all positions (unlike RNNs), but they suffer from a path length problem: the number of operations to relate two arbitrary positions grows with distance - linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. To connect any two positions, you need a stack of O(n/k) or O(log_k(n)) convolutional layers. The Transformer reduces path length to O(1) - any two positions are connected within a single self-attention operation. Convolutional layers are also generally more expensive than recurrent layers by a factor of k (kernel size). The Transformer outperforms ConvS2S on both EN-DE (27.3 vs 25.16 BLEU base) and EN-FR translation tasks.
Where is layer normalisation applied in the Transformer and why?

Layer normalisation is applied after each sub-layer in both encoder and decoder, using the pattern LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). The residual connection x + Sublayer(x) allows gradients to flow directly through layers, preventing vanishing gradients in the deep 6-layer stack. All sub-layers and embedding layers produce outputs of d_model=512 so the residual addition is always dimensionally consistent. Layer normalisation rather than batch normalisation is used because it works on individual sequence elements regardless of batch size, and is more stable for variable-length sequence models. The combination of residual connections and layer normalisation is the standard pattern used throughout the Transformer.
What is label smoothing and what effect did it have on Transformer training?

Label smoothing (Szegedy et al., 2016) modifies the target distribution during training. Instead of training the model to output probability 1.0 for the correct token (hard target), the distribution is smoothed: the correct token gets probability (1 - epsilon_ls) = 0.9 and the remaining probability epsilon_ls = 0.1 is distributed uniformly across all other vocabulary tokens. This prevents the model from becoming overconfident. The effect is counterintuitive: label smoothing hurts perplexity (the model is trained to be more uncertain) but improves accuracy and BLEU score because overconfident models overfit while regularised models generalise better. The Transformer used epsilon_ls = 0.1.
What is the difference between additive attention and dot-product attention?

Additive attention computes compatibility scores using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer: score(q, k) = v^T tanh(W_1 q + W_2 k). Dot-product attention computes scores as q^T k (scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k) in the Transformer). Both have similar theoretical complexity. However, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice because it can be implemented with highly optimised matrix multiplication routines. For small d_k both mechanisms perform similarly. For large d_k, additive attention outperforms unscaled dot-product attention because large dot products push softmax into low-gradient regions. The Transformer addresses this with the scaling factor 1/sqrt(d_k) - the key contribution of Scaled Dot-Product Attention.
What changes were made in the big Transformer model compared to the base model?

The big Transformer differs from the base model as follows: d_model increased from 512 to 1024; d_ff increased from 2048 to 4096; number of heads h increased from 8 to 16; dropout rate P_drop increased from 0.1 to 0.3 (for EN-FR); training extended from 100,000 steps to 300,000 steps; total parameters increased from approximately 65 million to approximately 213 million. All other design choices remain the same: N=6 layers, label smoothing epsilon_ls=0.1, Adam optimizer with warmup. The big model achieved 28.4 BLEU on EN-DE and 41.8 BLEU on EN-FR, both state-of-the-art results at the time of publication.
In encoder-decoder attention, where do the queries, keys and values come from?

In encoder-decoder attention (the middle sub-layer of each decoder layer), the queries come from the output of the previous decoder layer, while the keys and values come from the output of the encoder stack. This asymmetry is deliberate: the decoder's current representation (query) needs to search the encoder output (keys/values) for the most relevant source context. Every decoder position can attend to every position in the input sequence - there is no masking in encoder-decoder attention. In contrast, encoder self-attention has all three (Q, K, V) coming from the encoder, and decoder self-attention has all three from the decoder (with masking to prevent attending to future positions).
What are the learned projection matrices in Multi-Head Attention and what are their shapes?

For each attention head i, there are three learned projection matrices: W^Q_i of shape (d_model, d_k), W^K_i of shape (d_model, d_k), and W^V_i of shape (d_model, d_v). These project the input from d_model dimensions down to d_k or d_v for each head. After the h heads are computed and concatenated (producing a h*d_v vector), a fourth output projection W^O of shape (h*d_v, d_model) projects back to d_model. In the base model: d_model=512, h=8, d_k=d_v=64. Each W^Q_i and W^K_i is 512x64, each W^V_i is 512x64, and W^O is 512x512. Total computation is similar to single-head attention at full d_model=512 dimensionality.
What was the broader significance of the Transformer paper and what future directions did the authors propose?

The Transformer was the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention, replacing the recurrent layers that had dominated sequence modelling. Its practical significance was immediate: state-of-the-art results on two major translation benchmarks at a fraction of prior training costs. The paper opened the research direction that led to BERT, GPT, T5, and virtually all modern large language models. The authors proposed extending the Transformer to modalities beyond text - images, audio, and video - and investigating local restricted attention for efficiently handling long sequences. They identified making generation less sequential as a research goal, anticipating future work on parallel decoding. Code was released at github.com/tensorflow/tensor2tensor.
What tokenisation approach did the Transformer paper use and why?

The Transformer used Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) for English-German and word-piece tokenisation for English-French. BPE iteratively merges the most frequent character pair until a target vocabulary size is reached. For English-German, a shared source-target vocabulary of approximately 37,000 BPE tokens was used. Sharing the vocabulary between source and target languages means the same embedding matrix is used for both, reducing parameters and allowing cross-lingual token overlap. For English-French, word-piece tokenisation with a 32,000-token vocabulary was used. Subword tokenisation addresses the open vocabulary problem: rare or unknown words are split into known subword units, ensuring every word can be represented without an unknown-token fallback.
Why are residual connections important in the Transformer?

Residual connections add the sub-layer input directly to the sub-layer output before layer normalisation: LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). They serve two functions. First, they create a gradient highway: during backpropagation, gradients can flow directly from the output through the addition to earlier layers without passing through the sub-layer transformation, preventing vanishing gradients in the 6-layer deep stack. Second, they allow the network to learn incremental refinements: each sub-layer only needs to learn the delta from the identity mapping, a simpler optimisation target. Residual connections also enforce that all sub-layers produce outputs of d_model=512, making the addition dimensionally consistent.
Summarise the Attention Is All You Need paper in 150 words or fewer.

The Transformer is a sequence-to-sequence model that replaces recurrent and convolutional layers with multi-head self-attention. The encoder and decoder are each 6-layer stacks. Each layer has a multi-head self-attention sub-layer, a position-wise feed-forward sub-layer, and residual connections with layer normalisation. Positional encodings (sinusoidal) inject token order information. Scaled Dot-Product Attention computes Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V; multi-head attention runs 8 such heads in parallel in 64-dimensional spaces. The decoder uses masking to enforce autoregression and adds an encoder-decoder attention sub-layer. Trained with Adam, a warmup learning rate schedule, dropout, and label smoothing, the base model (65M parameters) achieves 27.3 BLEU on English-German translation in 12 hours on 8 GPUs. The big model (213M parameters) achieves 28.4 BLEU, surpassing all prior models including ensembles.
What did the ablation studies show about the effect of the number of attention heads?

Table 3 rows (A) vary the number of attention heads while keeping total computation constant. Single-head attention (h=1) was 0.9 BLEU lower than the best setting (24.9 vs 25.8). Too many heads also hurt: h=32 (with d_k=16) dropped to 25.4 BLEU. The sweet spot was h=8. Reducing d_k while keeping h fixed (rows B) also hurt quality, suggesting that a richer compatibility function than a simple dot product might be beneficial when d_k is very small. Model size (rows C) and dropout (rows D) ablations confirmed that larger models and dropout both improve performance consistently.
Why was warmup necessary in the Transformer learning rate schedule?

At the very start of training, model parameters are randomly initialised and gradients are noisy and unreliable. A high learning rate at this stage can push parameters into poor regions that are hard to recover from. The warmup linearly increases the learning rate from near zero to a peak value over the first 4,000 training steps. This allows the model to first converge to a reasonable region with a small, conservative learning rate, after which the larger peak rate enables faster progress. The peak learning rate is d_model^{-0.5}, so smaller models use a higher peak rate. After the warmup, the rate decays as step^{-0.5}, providing a stable decay as the model approaches a minimum.
What is sequence transduction and what prior approaches did the Transformer improve upon?

Sequence transduction maps an input sequence of symbols to an output sequence of symbols, often of different length - machine translation is the primary example. Prior leading approaches used encoder-decoder architectures based on recurrent neural networks: LSTMs and GRUs with attention (Bahdanau et al. 2015, Luong et al. 2015, GNMT). These were strong but constrained by sequential computation. Convolutional alternatives - ByteNet, ConvS2S - improved parallelism but needed stacked layers for long-range dependencies. The Transformer improved upon all of these with pure self-attention for both encoding and decoding, achieving higher BLEU at lower training cost, and demonstrating that recurrence is not necessary for state-of-the-art sequence transduction.
What specific motivations led the Transformer authors to replace RNNs with self-attention?

Three primary motivations drove the design. (1) Parallelisation: RNNs compute h_t from h_{t-1}, making within-example parallelisation impossible - the fundamental bottleneck for modern GPU training. Self-attention computes all positions simultaneously. (2) Long-range dependency learning: in RNNs, a dependency between positions n steps apart requires information to propagate through n hidden state transitions with risk of gradient decay. Self-attention connects any two positions in O(1) operations. (3) Computational efficiency for typical sentence lengths: self-attention O(n^2*d) is faster than recurrent O(n*d^2) when n < d, which holds for sentences with d=512. Interpretability - individual attention heads learn specialised patterns - is a valuable side benefit.
How does the Transformer training cost compare to prior state-of-the-art models?

Table 2 compares BLEU and FLOPs. The base Transformer (27.3 EN-DE BLEU) used approximately 3.3e18 FLOPs - far less than ConvS2S (9.6e18 FLOPs, 25.16 BLEU) and GNMT+RL (2.3e19 FLOPs, 24.6 BLEU). The big Transformer (28.4 EN-DE, 41.8 EN-FR BLEU) used 2.3e19 FLOPs - the same order as GNMT+RL but with notably higher quality. The EN-FR result was achieved at less than 1/4 the training cost of the prior best single model. The combined results show the Transformer is not only more accurate but significantly more compute-efficient - a key practical advantage beyond the architectural novelty.
How does the Transformer relate to end-to-end memory networks?

End-to-end memory networks (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015) use a recurrent attention mechanism over an external memory rather than sequence-aligned recurrence, and demonstrated that attention over stored key-value memories can perform well on question answering. The Transformer can be seen as extending this insight: the encoder output functions as a memory bank (keys and values), and the decoder queries this memory at each step via encoder-decoder attention. However, the Transformer's novelty is applying self-attention within the encoder and decoder as well - using attention to compute the representations themselves, not just to retrieve from a fixed external memory. It is the first model to rely entirely on self-attention for computing input and output representations without sequence-aligned RNNs or convolutions.
Trace the information flow from an input sentence through the Transformer to produce the first output token.

Step 1 - Input embedding: each source token is converted to a 512-dim vector via the embedding layer. Positional encodings are added. Step 2 - Encoder stack: the embedded sequence passes through 6 encoder layers. In each layer, multi-head self-attention aggregates context from all positions, then the FFN processes each position independently. Residual connections and layer normalisation wrap each sub-layer. Step 3 - Encoder output: a sequence of 512-dim contextualised representations, one per source token. Step 4 - Decoder start: the decoder begins with the start-of-sequence token plus its positional encoding. Step 5 - Decoder layer: (a) masked self-attention over decoder input so far, (b) encoder-decoder attention queries the encoder keys/values, (c) FFN. Six such layers. Step 6 - Linear + softmax over vocabulary; beam search selects the first output token.
What does the paper say about the maximum path length comparison across layer types?

The maximum path length between any two input/output positions measures how many sequential operations a signal must traverse to propagate between positions. Short paths are critical for learning long-range dependencies because long gradient paths through many Jacobians are prone to vanishing or exploding. Self-attention achieves O(1) maximum path length - any two positions connect in one step. Recurrent layers require O(n) path length, meaning information from position 1 takes n steps to reach position n. Convolutional layers with kernel k require O(log_k(n)) (dilated) or O(n/k) (contiguous). O(1) path length in self-attention directly explains why the Transformer is more effective at capturing long-range dependencies than LSTM-based models on translation tasks.
What alternatives to sinusoidal positional encoding did the paper explore?

The paper tested learned positional embeddings as used in Gehring et al. (2017). Row (E) of Table 3 shows replacing sinusoidal encodings with learned positional embeddings produced nearly identical results: 25.7 BLEU vs 25.8 BLEU for the sinusoidal version. The authors chose the sinusoidal version because it can potentially extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training - for any fixed offset k, PE_{pos+k} can be expressed as a linear function of PE_{pos}. Learned embeddings only have parameters up to the maximum training sequence length. The sinusoidal choice provides a marginal robustness benefit at essentially zero performance cost.
What was the inference procedure used to generate Transformer translations?

For inference, beam search was used with beam size 4 and length penalty alpha=0.6, chosen by experimentation on the development set. Maximum output length was set to input length + 50 tokens, with early termination when possible. For the base models, the last 5 training checkpoints (written at 10-minute intervals) were averaged to form a single weight set before inference. For the big models, the last 20 checkpoints were averaged. Checkpoint averaging is a form of implicit ensembling that reduces variance without any additional inference cost, distinct from explicit model ensembling which requires multiple forward passes. The technique consistently improves quality at no runtime cost.
What are the authors of the Transformer paper and what were their specific contributions?

The paper has eight authors from Google Brain, Google Research, and the University of Toronto, all listed as equal contributors. Ashish Vaswani and Illia Polosukhin designed and implemented the first Transformer models. Noam Shazeer proposed scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, and the parameter-free positional representation. Jakob Uszkoreit proposed replacing RNNs with self-attention and initiated the evaluation effort. Niki Parmar designed, implemented, tuned and evaluated countless model variants in the original codebase and tensor2tensor. Llion Jones worked on model variants, the initial codebase, and efficient inference and visualisations. Lukasz Kaiser and Aidan N. Gomez designed and implemented tensor2tensor, replacing the earlier codebase and greatly improving results. The paper was presented at NIPS 2017 in Long Beach, CA.
What is byte-pair encoding and why was it important for the Transformer?

Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) is a subword tokenisation algorithm that starts with individual characters as vocabulary items, then iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new vocabulary item, until a target vocabulary size is reached. It produces a vocabulary of subword units - common words appear as single tokens, rare words are split into known subword pieces. For the Transformer's English-German task, a shared source-target BPE vocabulary of ~37,000 tokens was used. Sharing the vocabulary means the same embedding matrix covers both input and output tokens, reducing parameters and enabling cross-lingual transfer within the shared subword space. BPE eliminates unknown tokens since any word can always be decomposed into its constituent bytes at worst, ensuring full coverage.
Why does the Transformer share weights between embedding layers and the pre-softmax projection?

Three-way weight tying between the source embedding, target embedding, and pre-softmax linear transformation (following Press and Wolf, 2016) provides two benefits. First, it significantly reduces total parameter count - the vocabulary embedding matrix is the largest single weight matrix in the model (vocabulary_size x d_model), so tying three copies into one is a large reduction. Second, it forces the model to learn embeddings that are consistent in both the input representation space and the output probability prediction space. When a subword token is used as an input embedding, the same representation must also be useful for predicting that token as an output. This consistency regularises learning and empirically improves language model quality. The embedding weights are scaled by sqrt(d_model) before positional encoding addition.
How did the Transformer perform on the development set ablation experiments for model depth?

Table 3 rows (C) vary the number of encoder/decoder layers N while keeping other parameters fixed. N=2 gives 23.7 BLEU (perplexity 6.11, 36M parameters), N=4 gives 25.3 BLEU (5.19, 50M parameters), and N=8 gives 25.5 BLEU (4.88, 80M parameters). The base model with N=6 achieves 25.8 BLEU (4.92, 65M parameters). The pattern shows diminishing returns: each doubling of depth improves less. N=6 was the practical optimum balancing quality, training time, and memory at the target parameter count. The big model also uses N=6 but scales d_model and d_ff to 1024 and 4096 instead of adding more layers to reach 213M parameters.
Describe the complete architecture of a single Transformer decoder layer.

A single Transformer decoder layer contains three sub-layers, each wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalisation: LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). (1) Masked multi-head self-attention: applies multi-head attention with future-position masking. The queries, keys and values all come from the decoder's own previous layer output. Masking ensures position i cannot attend to positions j > i. (2) Encoder-decoder multi-head attention: queries come from the previous decoder layer; keys and values come from the final encoder output. No masking - every decoder position attends to every encoder position. (3) Position-wise feed-forward network: two linear layers with ReLU, d_model=512 in/out, d_ff=2048 inner. All sub-layers produce d_model=512-dimensional outputs to maintain consistent dimensionality for residual addition.
